description: Deterministic DNR match expectations, asserted against Chrome's own matcher via chrome.declarativeNetRequest.testMatchOutcome. A case states the request Chrome sees and whether the packaged rulesets must block it. Live ad serving is probabilistic; this is not.

cases.why: Alphabetically early generated rule. Was already covered before the rule cap was raised.
Past the old 5000-rule cut. Guards against the generated ruleset being truncated again.
Last generated rule alphabetically. EasyList's domain section is sorted, so a truncated build fails here first.
The video ad SDK is blocked by default.
EasyList exempts the SDK here because blocking it stops the player from starting the feature video, not just the ad.
Same carve-out for the dynamic-ad-insertion loader.
Google Publisher Tag is blocked by default.
EasyList exempts GPT here because blocking it breaks page layout.
Exception rules must be scoped to their initiator, never applied globally.
Preroll VAST tag. The network rotates hostnames, so this must be caught by the request path, not the host. A host rule here goes stale within weeks.
Same VAST endpoint shape on an unrelated host. If only one of the two rotating-host cases fails, the path rule was narrowed to a host by mistake.
The preroll video itself, served from the ad network's CDN once the VAST tag resolves.
Second creative CDN in the same chain.
The feature film's HLS manifest. Blocking the player CDN breaks playback entirely, which is worse than showing the ad.
Film video segments ride a rotating subdomain of the same player CDN.
The player bootstrap itself. Must survive any rule aimed at the ad chain.

The generator once wrote ||adnxs.com without the trailing ^ EasyList had, so the rule also matched any host merely beginning with it. One dropped character was a false positive on all 52k generated rules.
Same class without a dot boundary. An innocent host must not inherit a block because its name starts with a blocked one.
EasyList blocks this general-purpose CDN only on five named sites. The block must still fire on one of them.
The same rule everywhere else. Dropping a $domain= scope here would block a CDN that serves a large share of the ordinary web.
$third-party maps to domainType. The block must fire when the request really is third-party.
Ignoring $third-party would have blocked the site's own assets when a visitor goes there directly.
Host-plus-path rules. EasyList blocks this path rather than the host, and so must we.
Proves the path is load-bearing. If this blocks, a path rule was widened into a host rule.
Host-agnostic path rules are the shape that survives hostname rotation, which is what the preroll chain used to escape.
Same path on an unrelated host. If only one of the pair fails, the rule was anchored to a host by mistake.
An exception with no $domain= is still safe when its own path names one file. These were dropped entirely before.
The other half of the pair. An unscoped allow that leaked to the whole host would silently unblock a tracker everywhere.
Breaking CAPTCHAs locks people out of logins, which is the most expensive false positive an ad blocker can ship.
False-positive canary for a generated ruleset this large.
False-positive canary on a first-party asset host.
